paraphrase: Makkhali Gosāla says: there is no cause or condition for the defilement of beings or for their purification; there is no doing by oneself or by another, no human doing, no power, no energy, no human strength or vigour. All beings, all living things, all creatures, all souls are without control, power or energy; transformed by destiny, circumstance and nature (niyati-saṅgati-bhāva-pariṇatā), they experience pleasure and pain in the six classes (abhijāti). There is no ripening of unripe karma or wearing out of ripe karma by conduct, vows, austerity or the holy life; pleasure and pain are measured out as with a measure and saṃsāra is fixed in its limits, with no increase or decrease. As a ball of string, thrown, runs out unwinding, so fool and wise alike, having run and wandered through saṃsāra, will make an end of suffering. The king calls this 'purification through transmigration' (saṃsāra-suddhi).

paraphrase: Ajita Kesakambalī says: there is no gift, no sacrifice, no offering, no fruit or result of good and bad deeds, no this world, no other world, no mother, no father, no spontaneously born beings, no ascetics or brahmins in the world who, rightly practising, declare this world and the other from their own direct knowledge. Four men with the bier as fifth carry the corpse; the footprints show as far as the burning-ground; the bones turn the colour of doves; offerings end in ashes. Giving is a doctrine of fools; the talk of those who assert existence is empty lying. Fool and wise alike are annihilated and destroyed at the breaking of the body and do not exist after death. paraphrase: The chieftain Pāyāsi holds the view: 'there is no other world, there are no spontaneously born beings, there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds'.

paraphrase: Pāyāsi's arguments: his wicked relatives, told they would go to hell, and his virtuous relatives, told they would go to heaven, promised to return and tell him, but none came back or sent a messenger; and virtuous ascetics who want to live and fear death do not kill themselves to reach the heaven they believe in. Kumāra Kassapa answers with similes: a condemned bandit is not allowed leave to visit his kin; a man pulled from a cesspit would not wish to go back into it; a day in the Thirty-three is a century here; the blind from birth deny colours; and a pregnant woman who cuts open her belly to hasten the birth destroys herself and the child — the virtuous do not force the unripe to ripen.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Pāyāsi Sutta (DN 23). Section refs = SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation, checked in the local e-text.

paraphrase: Pāyāsi's experiments on condemned criminals: one was sealed alive in a jar and heated, and on opening no soul was seen leaving; one was weighed alive and weighed after being strangled, and was heavier dead; one was killed without harming skin, flesh or bone, and no soul was seen leaving; one was cut open layer by layer, and no soul was seen. Kassapa answers: you do not see the soul of a dreaming man going and coming; a hot iron ball is lighter than a cold one, as a body with life, warmth and consciousness is lighter; a conch sounds only when blown by a man; and the boy who split the fire-sticks to find fire never found it.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Pāyāsi Sutta (DN 23). Section refs = SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation, checked in the local e-text. Closely parallel to King Paesi's experiments in the Jain Rājapraśnīya.

paraphrase: Pāyāsi says he will not give up his view for fear of what people would say; Kassapa tells of the man who, carrying hemp, would not exchange it for linen, silver or gold. Pāyāsi then admits he was delighted with the very first simile and argued only to hear more, and takes refuge.
speaker: Kumāra Kassapa

paraphrase: If one holds 'the soul is the same as the body' there is no living of the holy life; if one holds 'the soul is one thing, the body another' there is no living of the holy life. Avoiding both extremes the Tathāgata teaches by the middle: with ignorance as condition, formations, and so on.
speaker: the Buddha

paraphrase: Some ascetics hold that whatever a person feels is due to past deeds; by burning up old deeds through austerity and doing no new ones, deeds, suffering and feeling come to an end. 'Such is the doctrine of the Nigaṇṭhas.' The Buddha questions them and shows the doctrine does not hold.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Buddha (MN 101, Buddhist Pali canon). Section refs = SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation, checked in the local e-text. A Buddhist report of the Jain doctrine; U34/U35 give the Jain account.

paraphrase: There are ascetics and brahmins who say 'purity comes through transmigration'. The Buddha: it is not easy to find a realm not already passed through in this long time, except the Pure Abodes, from which he would not have returned.
speaker: the Buddha
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Buddha (MN 12, Buddhist Pali canon). Section refs = SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation, checked in the local e-text. The doctrine is Makkhali's in DN 2; MN 12 names no one. The same passage rejects purity through food, rebirth, abode, sacrifice and fire-worship.

paraphrase: The naked ascetic Kassapa lists the ascetic practices held to make one an ascetic or brāhmaṇa: going naked, licking the hands, refusing food brought or prepared, refusing food at certain times and places, restricted foods, eating at long intervals, wearing coarse garments, pulling out hair and beard, standing, squatting, lying on thorns, bathing thrice daily. The Buddha answers that one who does all this but has not developed ethics, mind and wisdom is far from being an ascetic or brāhmaṇa.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Buddha and Kassapa (DN 8, Buddhist Pali canon). Section refs = SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation, checked in the local e-text. Summary only; the text's fasting intervals are not reproduced here.

paraphrase: Puṇṇa, who keeps the cow-vow, and Seniya, a naked ascetic who keeps the dog-vow and eats food thrown on the ground, ask about each other's destiny. The Buddha, after hesitation, says one who develops the dog-vow fully, with a dog's mind and habits, is reborn among dogs if it succeeds; if he holds that by it he will become a god, that is wrong view and leads to hell or the animal realm. The same holds for the cow-vow.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Buddha (MN 57, Buddhist Pali canon). Section refs = SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation, checked in the local e-text.

paraphrase: On the road between Gayā and Bodhgayā the Ājīvaka Upaka sees the newly awakened Buddha, remarks that his faculties are clear and his complexion bright, and asks who his teacher is. The Buddha declares himself self-awakened, without a teacher, the victor; Upaka says 'may it be so, friend', shakes his head and takes a by-path.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Buddha's own narration (MN 26, Buddhist Pali canon). Section refs = SuttaCentral (bilara) segmentation, checked in the local e-text. Also Vinaya Mv 1.6.7–9.

paraphrase: Sañjaya the wanderer lived at Rājagaha with 250 wanderers, among them Sāriputta and Moggallāna. After Sāriputta heard the verse on causes from Assaji, the two went to the Buddha with the 250; Sañjaya refused to come, and hot blood gushed from his mouth.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Vinaya Mahāvagga (Buddhist Pali canon). SuttaCentral pli-tv-kd1:23–24. The Vinaya calls him only 'Sañjaya the wanderer'.

paraphrase: A Rājagaha merchant hung a sandalwood bowl on a bamboo pole for 'any ascetic or brahmin who is an arahant with powers'. Pūraṇa Kassapa, Makkhali Gosāla, Ajita, Pakudha, Sañjaya and the Nigaṇṭha each came claiming 'I am an arahant with powers — give me the bowl', and were told to take it down; Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja rose into the air and took it. The Buddha rebuked him and forbade monks to display superhuman powers to lay people.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Vinaya Cullavagga (Buddhist Pali canon). SuttaCentral pli-tv-kd15:8. The rebuke is recalled from the same section; the local check confirmed the six teachers' claims.

paraphrase: One who has calmed (sameti) all evils, small and great, is called a samaṇa because of the calming of evils.

paraphrase: One who has put away evil is called a brāhmaṇa; one who lives in calm (samacariyā) is called a samaṇa; one who has driven out his own stain is called 'gone forth' (pabbajita).

paraphrase: Even if adorned, one who lives in calm, tamed, restrained, chaste, having laid down the rod toward all beings — he is a brāhmaṇa, he is a samaṇa, he is a bhikkhu.

paraphrase: Patient endurance is the highest austerity; nibbāna is supreme, say the Buddhas; one who harms another is not gone forth, one who hurts another is no samaṇa.

paraphrase: Verses of Cāpā: her husband Kāḷa, formerly an ascetic carrying a staff, now hunting deer, says he will cut her bonds and go forth again; she pleads with him, he leaves, and goes to the Buddha.
notes: SuttaCentral thig13.3. The verses name the man Kāḷa; the commentary identifies him with Upaka the Ājīvaka (not in the verses).

paraphrase: The naked ascetic Guṇa of the Kassapa clan teaches King Aṅgati: there is no fruit, good or bad, of living by dharma; there is no other world — who has come back from it?; there are no ancestors, no mother or father, no teacher to tame the untamed; beings are all equal, there is no honouring of elders; there is no strength or energy, still less effort; beings are fixed (niyatāni) like the stern-rope of a boat; a man gets what he is to get, so what fruit has giving? Giving was laid down by fools. Seven bodies are eternal and cannot be cut — fire, earth, water, air, pleasure, pain and soul — so the sword only passes between them; all are purified by wandering through 84 great aeons, and before that time even the restrained is not purified: 'we do not pass beyond destiny, as the ocean does not pass its shore'.
notes: Reported by an opponent: a Buddhist Jātaka (Ja 544 Fausbøll / SC ja545). SuttaCentral verse segments 34–45, checked locally.

paraphrase: If Brahmā is lord of the whole world, master of beings, why did he order the world to misfortune and not make it happy? Why did he make it with deceit, lies and pride, and without justice? The lord of beings is unjust who, where there is dharma, ordained adharma.
speaker: Bhūridatta (the Bodhisatta)
notes: SuttaCentral ja543 verse segments, checked locally.

paraphrase: Bhūridatta rejects the brāhmaṇas' claims: if the one who kills in sacrifice is purified and the victim goes to heaven, let brāhmaṇas kill brāhmaṇas; animals do not ask to be killed; the sacrificial post does not yield wishes; the priests are like crows mobbing an owl, cheats who take the seen for the unseen.
speaker: Bhūridatta
notes: SuttaCentral ja543 segments 161–173, checked locally.

paraphrase: King Milinda asks Pūraṇa Kassapa who protects the world; Pūraṇa says 'the earth protects the world'; asked why beings going to Avīci hell pass beyond the earth, he can neither swallow nor spit out the question and sits silent.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Milindapañha (Buddhist Pali canon). SuttaCentral mil2 segment 7 (Bāhirakathā), checked locally in Pali. The six are here anachronistically contemporaries of Milinda.

paraphrase: Milinda asks Makkhali Gosāla whether there are good and bad deeds and their fruit; Gosāla says there are none: those who are khattiyas, brāhmaṇas, vessas, suddas, caṇḍālas or pukkusas here will be the same in the next world. Milinda asks whether then one whose hand is cut off here will have it cut off there too; Gosāla falls silent.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Milindapañha (Buddhist Pali canon). SuttaCentral mil2 segment 8, checked locally.

paraphrase: At the time of the Twin Miracle at Sāvatthī the rival teachers were put to shame; Pūraṇa Kassapa, disgraced, tied a pot of sand to his neck and drowned himself in a pond.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Dhammapada commentary (Theravāda). Story location and details from memory; verify.

paraphrase: Buddhaghosa explains the six names: Pūraṇa, a slave, 'completed' a hundred slaves; Makkhali, told 'don't stumble' (mā khali) while carrying an oil-pot, ran off naked; Ajita wore a blanket of human hair; he glosses Makkhali's lists, including the 'eight stages of a person' as stages of life from the dull newborn to the one who has gone forth and beyond.
notes: Reported by an opponent: Buddhaghosa (Theravāda commentary). From memory; not verified locally.

paraphrase: The six tīrthika teachers, losing support to the Buddha, challenge him to a contest of wonders at Śrāvastī; the Buddha performs the great miracle and the tīrthikas are routed; Pūraṇa drowns himself.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Divyāvadāna (Mūlasarvāstivāda legend). Prātihārya-sūtra; details from memory.

paraphrase: In the Aśoka cycle, when a follower of the Nirgrantha at Puṇḍravardhana drew the Buddha bowing at the Nirgrantha's feet, Aśoka ordered the Ājīvikas there to be killed; later his own brother Vītāśoka was killed in a similar persecution, after which Aśoka forbade such killing.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Divyāvadāna (Buddhist legend). Recalled with low confidence (Vītāśokāvadāna); versions differ between Ājīvika and Nirgrantha. A legend, not a historical record; recorded as the tradition's account.

paraphrase: The king honours all sects, ascetics and householders alike, with gifts and honours, but values most the growth of their essentials; its root is restraint of speech — not praising one's own sect or disparaging another's without cause; one who praises his own sect out of devotion harms it; concord (samavāya) is good, that all may hear and follow one another's dharma.
speaker: Aśoka (Piyadasi)
notes: Rock Edict 12 (Girnār/Shāhbāzgarhī versions); paraphrase from memory of standard translations.

paraphrase: There is no land, except among the Greeks, where these orders — brāhmaṇas and śramaṇas — are not found, and none where people do not hold to some sect.
speaker: Aśoka
notes: Rock Edict 13; from memory.

paraphrase: The dhamma-mahāmātras are appointed to the affairs of the Saṅgha, of the brāhmaṇas, of the Ājīvikas, of the Nigaṇṭhas, and of the various other sects.
speaker: Aśoka
notes: Pillar Edict 7 (Delhi–Topra); from memory.

paraphrase: Gosāla was the son of Maṅkhali, a picture-showman (maṅkha), and Bhaddā, born in the cowshed of the brāhmaṇa Gobahula at Saravaṇa, hence his name. In the second year of Mahāvīra's asceticism he attached himself to Mahāvīra at Nālandā as a disciple, and they wandered together for six years.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Bhagavatī Sūtra, book 15 (Jain canon). Not available locally; narrative recalled from memory of the text and its translations — details to verify.

paraphrase: During their wandering Gosāla uprooted a sesame plant that Mahāvīra had said would bear pods; when it re-rooted and bore seeds as foretold, Gosāla concluded that all living beings are capable of reanimation (pauṭṭa-parihāra) — of dying and returning in the same or another body. Mahāvīra saved him with his cooling power from the fiery power (tejoleśyā) hurled at him by the ascetic Vesiyāyaṇa, whom Gosāla had mocked, and on his asking taught him how that fiery power is gained.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Bhagavatī Sūtra, book 15 (Jain canon). Not available locally; narrative recalled from memory of the text and its translations — details to verify. The method of gaining tejoleśyā (a course of severe fasting and exposure) is restricted: summary only.

paraphrase: After leaving Mahāvīra, Gosāla gained the fiery power and learned the eightfold Mahānimitta (prognostication) from six 'wanderers of the directions' (disācara) who had extracted it from the Pūrvas; with it he could foretell gain and loss, pleasure and pain, life and death, and he proclaimed himself a Jina.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Bhagavatī Sūtra, book 15 (Jain canon). Not available locally; narrative recalled from memory of the text and its translations — details to verify.

paraphrase: Sixteen years before Mahāvīra's death, at Sāvatthī, Gosāla, living in the pottery of Hālāhalā, heard that Mahāvīra called him merely Maṅkhali's son and his former disciple. He warned Mahāvīra's disciple Ānanda with the parable of the merchants who, not content with the treasure of three anthills, broke open a fourth and were burnt by the glance of a serpent; then he confronted Mahāvīra, saying that the disciple Gosāla was dead and that he was Udāyi Kuṇḍiyāyaṇa, who had entered Gosāla's body as the seventh of his reanimations. He burnt two monks who rebuked him with his fiery power; the fire he hurled at Mahāvīra circled him and turned back into Gosāla's own body. Each foretold the other's death.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Bhagavatī Sūtra, book 15 (Jain canon). Not available locally; narrative recalled from memory of the text and its translations — details to verify. The two monks are named Savvāṇubhūi and Sunakkhatta (recalled, moderate); the number and names of the prior bodies in Gosāla's claim are not reproduced here.

paraphrase: In his last days, burning with fever, Gosāla drank, sang, danced, repeatedly saluted Hālāhalā and sprinkled himself with clay-water; his followers explained these as the 'eight finalities' (carima): the last drink, last song, last dance, last salutation, the last great storm-cloud, the last sprinkling elephant, the last great battle of stones and thorns, and Gosāla himself as the last tīrthaṅkara of this age. He also taught four kinds of drink permitted and four not permitted (pāṇaga / apāṇaga), and answered the Ājīvika layman Ayampula's question in his delirium.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Bhagavatī Sūtra, book 15 (Jain canon). Not available locally; narrative recalled from memory of the text and its translations — details to verify. The list of finalities is recalled with moderate confidence; the drinks are not itemised here (not recalled reliably).

paraphrase: On the seventh night Gosāla came to his senses, confessed that he was indeed Maṅkhali's son, Mahāvīra's disciple and not a Jina, that he had destroyed ascetics, and asked his followers to tie a rope to his left foot, drag his corpse through Sāvatthī and proclaim his falsity; the Ājīvikas performed this only symbolically inside the closed pottery and then gave him a great funeral.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Bhagavatī Sūtra, book 15 (Jain canon). Not available locally; narrative recalled from memory of the text and its translations — details to verify.

paraphrase: Mahāvīra foretells Gosāla's destiny: reborn as a god in the Accuya heaven, then through a long series of births and hells, he will at last be born as Daḍhapaiṇṇa, attain omniscience and liberation.
speaker: Mahāvīra
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Bhagavatī Sūtra, book 15 (Jain canon). Not available locally; narrative recalled from memory of the text and its translations — details to verify.

paraphrase: The fiery power left Mahāvīra ill with a burning fever and bloody flux for six months; he was cured by a remedy fetched by the monk Sīha from the laywoman Revatī.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Bhagavatī Sūtra, book 15 (Jain canon). Not available locally; narrative recalled from memory of the text and its translations — details to verify. The wording of the remedy is a well-known crux of Jain exegesis; left to U34.

paraphrase: A god appears to the Jain layman Kuṇḍakoliya and praises the teaching of Gosāla Maṅkhaliputta — that there is no exertion, action, strength, energy or human effort, and all things are fixed (niyayā savvabhāvā) — over Mahāvīra's. Kuṇḍakoliya asks how the god gained his divine state: by exertion or without? If without, why are all beings not gods? The god falls silent; Mahāvīra praises the layman.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Uvāsagadasāo (Jain canon). Not available locally; from memory.

paraphrase: Saddālaputta, a rich Ājīvika potter of Polāsapura, holds Gosāla's doctrine: 'there is no exertion, action, strength, energy or human effort; all things are fixed'. Mahāvīra asks how his pots are made — by effort or without? — and whether he would punish a man who stole or broke his pots or assaulted his wife Aggimittā. Since he would, he does not in fact hold that there is no effort; he becomes Mahāvīra's lay follower.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Uvāsagadasāo (Jain canon). Not available locally; from memory.

paraphrase: Gosāla comes to win Saddālaputta back and praises Mahāvīra as the great brāhmaṇa, great cowherd, great guide, great preacher and great pilot; Saddālaputta gives him lodging but not as a teacher, and Gosāla cannot shake him.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Uvāsagadasāo (Jain canon). Not available locally; from memory.

paraphrase: Some say there are five great elements — earth, water, fire, air and space as fifth; from them arises a single (self), and with their destruction the embodied one is destroyed.

paraphrase: As one earth-mound appears manifold, so, some say, the one knower (viṇṇu) appears manifold throughout the whole world; the Jain text calls these the words of dull men attached to violence.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Jain canon). Verse numbers per the local GRETIL Suyagaḍa e-text (Book 1), checked. Commentators identify this as an Upaniṣadic one-self view.

paraphrase: Some say each self is complete (in its body), whether fool or wise; they exist, but after death they do not; there are no spontaneously born beings, no merit or demerit, no world beyond this; with the destruction of the body the embodied one is destroyed.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Jain canon). Verse numbers per the local GRETIL Suyagaḍa e-text (Book 1), checked. Śīlāṅka names this the tajjīva-taccharīra view.

paraphrase: Some boldly say that the self does not act or cause action: 'thus the self is a non-agent'; the Jain text says such teachers go from darkness to darkness.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Jain canon). Verse numbers per the local GRETIL Suyagaḍa e-text (Book 1), checked. Commentators identify it with Sāṃkhya.

paraphrase: Some say there are five great elements and the self is a sixth, and that self and world are eternal: neither perishes, the non-existent does not arise, all things are of a fixed nature.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Jain canon). Verse numbers per the local GRETIL Suyagaḍa e-text (Book 1), checked.

paraphrase: Some fools speak of five aggregates lasting a moment, neither different nor the same (as the self), caused and uncaused; others say form is the four elements earth, water, fire and air.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Jain canon). Verse numbers per the local GRETIL Suyagaḍa e-text (Book 1), checked. A Jain report of Buddhist views.

paraphrase: Each of these teachers claims that whoever adopts his view, at home, in the forest or as a renouncer, is freed from all suffering; the Jain text replies that they know neither the joint nor the dharma, do not cross the flood, saṃsāra, womb, birth, suffering or death, and wander again and again — so taught Nāyaputta Mahāvīra.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga. Verse numbers per the local GRETIL Suyagaḍa e-text (Book 1), checked.

paraphrase: Some teach that beings, arising separately, experience pleasure and pain or lose their place, but that this suffering is neither self-made nor made by others: whether pleasure or pain, gained at the right time or not, it is determined by circumstance (saṅgaiya). The Jain text calls those who say this fools who think themselves wise, not knowing what is fixed and what is not fixed, and not freed from suffering.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Jain canon). Verse numbers per the local GRETIL Suyagaḍa e-text (Book 1), checked. Commentators identify this as the Ājīvika niyativāda; the word saṅgaiya echoes DN 2's niyati-saṅgati-bhāva.

paraphrase: Some brāhmaṇas and śramaṇas each claim knowledge, yet know nothing of the beings in the world; like a barbarian repeating a non-barbarian's words without their meaning, the ignorant (annāṇiya) do not know the settled meaning; the inquiry of the ignorant cannot be settled in ignorance — unable to instruct themselves, how can they instruct others? Like a man lost in a forest following a guide equally lost, or the blind leading the blind, reasoners who follow their own speculation cannot escape suffering, like a bird from its cage.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Jain canon). Verse numbers per the local GRETIL Suyagaḍa e-text (Book 1), checked.

paraphrase: Another view, the kiriyāvāda of those 'who have left behind concern with karma': sin is incurred only by three means — acting oneself, commissioning another, and approving in mind; what is done unknowingly or without intent is not fully binding; purified by the intention within, one reaches nirvāṇa; even a father who, in need, kills and eats his son is not stained. The Jain text replies that those who sin in mind are not free of thought, and that such teachers are not restrained.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Jain canon). Verse numbers per the local GRETIL Suyagaḍa e-text (Book 1), checked. Commentators identify it as a Buddhist doctrine of intention.

paraphrase: Some say the world was made by the gods, others by Brahmā, by Īśvara, by the primal matter (pradhāna), by the self-born one (with the delusion spread by Māra, so that the world is impermanent), or that the world came from an egg; the Jain text says they do not know the truth — the world never perishes — and, not knowing the origin of suffering, cannot know how to stop it.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Jain canon). Verse numbers per the local GRETIL Suyagaḍa e-text (Book 1), checked.

paraphrase: Some say the self is pure and sinless, yet through fondness for play (kiḍḍā-padosa) it falls again into fault; one who has become a restrained muni here later becomes sinless, 'as clear water becomes muddy and then clear again'.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Jain canon). Verse numbers per the local GRETIL Suyagaḍa e-text (Book 1), checked. Commentators (Śīlāṅka, recalled with low confidence) ascribe this to the Trairāśikas, whom they identify with Gosāla's followers: the liberated soul returns to saṃsāra. The term khiḍḍāpadosika also names gods in DN 1.

paraphrase: There are four 'assemblies' (samosaraṇa) in which the disputants (pāvāduya) each speak: action (kiriya), non-action (akiriya), discipline (viṇaya) as third, and ignorance (annāṇa) as fourth.

notes: Reported by an opponent: Jayanta Bhaṭṭa, Nyāyamañjarī (Nyāya). Āhnika 1, checked. The description fits Jayarāśi's method; Jayanta names no one.

paraphrase: The well-educated Cārvāka says: let there be one knower lasting as long as the body, capable of recollection — who quarrels about that? But what proof is there that it exists beyond the body? The knower does not pass from the former body to another, for then it would remember its past births as it remembers childhood; so give up the fairy-tale of the other world rooted in the eternal-self doctrine and live at ease: 'while life lasts let one live happily; none is beyond death's reach; once the body is burnt to ashes, how can it return?' Jayanta replies that, having granted a knower lasting through the body, he cannot show a cause of its destruction, so it is eternal.

paraphrase: Some wrong-viewed people say that inference is not a means of knowledge — yet in saying so with words they convey their intention, which is itself known by inference.

paraphrase: The Lokāyata case: if no continuing entity exists, there is no other world, for there is no one to go there; body, mind and senses perish every moment and nothing else is admitted; therefore from particular elements, as the power of fermented liquor, cognition is produced or manifested; the elements in a particular arrangement are called body and senses, and there is no other principle; cognitions in different bodies are not cause and effect; the dying mind of one with passion does not link to another mind; so 'cognition arises from the body alone, sustained by in-breath and out-breath' — as Kambalāśvatara said.

paraphrase: Some Lokāyatikas, who see the self in the body alone and deny a self apart from it, hold that although consciousness is not seen in earth and the other external elements, singly or together, it may arise in them when transformed into the shape of a body; they say 'from them, consciousness', 'cognition is like intoxicating power', 'the person is the body qualified by consciousness'; there is no self apart from the body able to go to heaven or to liberation; their reason: (consciousness) exists where the body exists — what exists when something exists and not otherwise is its property, as heat and light are of fire.

paraphrase: The Lokāyatikas, not seeing a self that passes from this world to the next, denied it and so taught non-self in a wrong way ('the person is only as much as the range of the senses'); the Buddhas taught self for some, non-self for others, and for others neither self nor non-self.

Great Delusion says the doctrine was composed by Bṛhaspati and handed to Cārvāka, who spread it through his pupils.

paraphrase: Asked by Maṇimēkalai 'who is your lord and what are the principles of your text?', Pūraṇaṉ, who knows the Ājīvaka texts, answers: the lord is the boundless knower who is present in all things everywhere and always; the principles are five — life (uyir) and four kinds of atom (earth, water, fire, air); the atoms are beginningless and indestructible, never newly born, never entering one another or changing kind, never splitting; they combine into mountains, trees and bodies and separate again, and the knowing of them is called life; a single atom is seen only by the divine eye. Beings pass through six births — black, dark blue, green, red, golden and white — and, born in due order, reach release in the supremely white birth; gain and loss, meeting and parting, pleasure and pain, birth and death are all fixed while in the womb. 'This is the kind of the Maṟkali text.'

paraphrase: The Bhūtavādin says: as intoxication arises when dhātakī flowers, jaggery and other ingredients are combined, so consciousness arises in the elements, and when the elements break up it perishes, like the sound of a drum dying away; some elements are joined to life and consciousness, some are not; this is the true doctrine, the Lokāyata's understanding: perception alone is a means of knowledge, inference fails; this life and its fruit are in this birth alone; another world and the experiencing of the fruit of deeds there are false. Maṇimēkalai laughs: how does he know his own father and mother except by inference?
